summary: Summation No. 26 covers November 1947 (with many statistics for September and October) in four parts: General, Political, Economic and Social. The month was dominated by the Katayama coalition's fight to pass the Bill for Temporary State Control of Coal Mines, which split the Democratic Party under Shidehara, and by the dismissal of Agriculture Minister Hirano under Article 68. The Diet passed Supplementary Budget No. 7 (about 85.6 billion yen) with a drastic tax revision, and the 1,800-yen standard wage came under pressure from Central Labor Relations Committee rulings in the communications and railway disputes. Labor legislation advanced with the Unemployment Allowance, Unemployment Insurance and Employment Security Laws. Economic sections record record coal output (2,422,000 tons), the dissolution of the agricultural associations, price decontrol and staple-food price rises. The war crimes section reproduces defense testimony before the Tokyo Tribunal for Koiso, Matsui, Minami, Muto, Oka and Oshima, useful for historians of the trials, the purge, labor and the economic recovery programme.
highlights: The Bill for Temporary State Control of Coal Mines passed the House of Representatives 233 to 155 on 25 November after the Democratic Party split, with 24 members of Shidehara's faction voting against and later forming the Doshi Club.

On 4 November Prime Minister Katayama dismissed Agriculture and Forestry Minister Rikizo Hirano, the first use of the Article 68 power to remove a minister, deepening divisions in the Social Democratic Party.
Supplementary Budget No. 7 of 85,602,368,000 yen was approved by the Diet on 29 November with a tax revision aiming at 133,240,000,000 yen in 1947-48 taxes, including a levy on undamaged houses.

The Diet enacted the Unemployment Allowance and Unemployment Insurance Laws on 21 November, covering over 7,000,000 workers in firms of five or more, with insurance benefits starting 1 May 1948, plus the Employment Security Law.

The Diet dissolved the government-dominated agricultural associations (11,000 associations, 55,000 practice associations, over 40,000,000,000 yen assets) on 7 November, with a deadline of 15 August 1948 and a legal basis for voluntary cooperatives.

October coal production reached 2,422,000 metric tons, the highest of the Occupation, while the Central Labor Relations Committee ruled on 14 November that government wages should be raised above the 1,800-yen standard.

War crimes data showed 397 suspects tried, 380 found guilty and 33 sentenced to death; the Tokyo Tribunal heard defense cases for Koiso, Matsui, Minami, Muto, Oka and Oshima, with Maj. Gen. Myron C. Cramer acting president from 8 November.

Repatriation brought 46,589 Japanese home between 31 October and 27 November, 43,424 of them from Soviet and Soviet-controlled areas, and price controls on about 200 minor commodities ended 27 October.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover, table of contents for Parts I-IV and the list of charts, maps and graphs numbered 1 to 104.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Digest of November: no change in SCAP organization, the coal bill and Hirano dismissal, record coal output, an 85.6 billion yen budget, and new social security laws.

sections.title: Section 1. Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: No change occurred in the nonmilitary organization of General Headquarters, SCAP, during November.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Activities
sections.summary: Coal bill passed 233 to 155 on 25 November, Hirano removed 4 November, Heima Hayashi purged 26 November, Domestic Relations Court Law enacted, and 61 atrocity investigations completed.

sections.title: Section 3. Economic Activities
sections.summary: Agricultural associations dissolved 7 November, October coal at 2,422,000 tons, Supplementary Budget No. 7 approved 29 November, price controls lifted on 200 minor items, and new labor laws.

sections.title: Section 4. Social Activities
sections.summary: Typhus immunization on Hokkaido, public assistance raised 10 percent on 1 November, Child Welfare Law of 21 November, education conferences, and first Book Week on 17 November.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: The coal bill and budget fights, party realignment, the purge, public safety statistics, and Tokyo Tribunal defense testimony for six accused.

sections.title: Section 1. Government and Politics
sections.summary: Coal bill passed the lower house 233 to 155, the Democratic Party split under Shidehara, Hirano was dismissed, and 19,709 persons were screened in the purge.

sections.title: Political Developments
sections.summary: Coal bill stalemate, the 11 November leaders' agreement, passage on 25 November, and Supplementary Budget No. 7 introduced 1 November with a tax revision aiming at 133,240,000,000 yen.

sections.title: Political Parties
sections.summary: Hirano removed under Article 68, a Liberal drive of 9 November for a new conservative party, and the Shidehara faction's split from the Democrats into the Doshi Club.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: By 30 November the First National Diet had received 140 Cabinet bills, seven member bills and five committee bills, and enacted 65.

sections.title: The Purge
sections.summary: 19,709 persons screened 26 October to 28 November, Heima Hayashi purged 26 November, and 16 information media organizations blacklisted on 25 November.

sections.title: Section 2. Public Safety
sections.summary: Economic Police found 19,885,253 yen of hoarded goods in October; 181,915 offenses in September; prisons held 83,875; 868 fires; Akita Prison fire on 12 November.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal Affairs and War Crimes
sections.summary: Two judicial laws enacted, 61 investigations completed, 397 war criminals tried to date, and defense testimony before the Tokyo Tribunal for six accused.

sections.title: Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Diet enacted the Domestic Relations Court Law and Sea Casualties Inquiry Law; the Supreme Court heard three constitutional review cases, with decisions due in December.

sections.title: Investigation of Suspected War Criminals
sections.summary: Sixty-one atrocity investigations completed in the 30 days to 24 November, leaving 1,446 cases on hand, including 451 B-29 flyer cases.

sections.title: Apprehension of Suspected War Criminals
sections.summary: Japan ordered to apprehend 11 persons for delivery to Sugamo; 34 statuses clarified; 39 suspects interned, bringing the total interned to 1,036.

sections.title: Prosecution of War Criminals
sections.summary: 397 suspects tried to 30 November, 380 guilty and 33 sentenced to death; seven trials of 12 accused completed, including life imprisonment for Lt. Col. Mori.

sections.title: International Prosecution of War Criminals
sections.summary: Court sat 18 days in November; Maj. Gen. Myron C. Cramer became acting president on 8 November while Sir William Webb was in Australia.

sections.title: Defense of Kuniaki Koiso
sections.summary: Koiso testified on his 1945 Miao Pin peace overture to Chungking and his Cabinet's resignation on 5 April 1945; prosecution introduced Toda's document on Manchukuo advisers.

sections.title: Defense of Iwane Matsui
sections.summary: Witnesses Ouchi, Wakizaka and Okada described orderly conduct at Nanking; Matsui denied knowing of atrocities and said he lacked authority over army discipline.

sections.title: Defense of Jiro Minami
sections.summary: Nakamura's affidavit, September 1931 telegrams urging nonexpansion, Kodama on the Korean Army's border crossing, and Shidehara's testimony on the Mukden Incident.

sections.title: Defense of Akira Muto
sections.summary: Opening statement on Muto's four periods of service; Yamamoto testified on the General Staff's 16 November 1941 war plan that Muto handed to the Foreign Office.

sections.title: Defense of Takasumi Oka
sections.summary: Oikawa and Nomura testified that Oka, as Naval Affairs Bureau director, only supplied information at conferences; Oka said the Navy sought to avert war.

sections.title: Defense of Hiroshi Oshima
sections.summary: Wakamatsu, Kasahara and Usami testified on the 1935-39 Japan-Germany treaty talks; Oshima could not recall Ribbentrop's 29 November 1941 pledge to join a war on the United States.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Thirteen sections of production, trade, labor, finance and science data for September and October, with record coal output, new labor laws, price revisions and budget figures.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Cooperative Association laws of 7 November dissolve 11,000 associations; land sales reach 111,714 cho; October fish landings 110,952 tons; antarctic whaling fleets sail 6 November.

sections.title: Section 2. Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: October log output 468,248,000 board feet; coal 2,422,000 metric tons, an Occupation high; coal mine employment 486,681; crude oil 17,607 kiloliters; 12 of 30 minerals gained.

sections.title: Section 3. Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke fell to 165,930 tons, pig iron 30,385 tons, ammonium sulfate reached 61,771 tons, 8,409 coal-miners' houses built, and machine tool output stayed low at 435 units.

sections.title: Coke
sections.summary: October coke fell to 165,930 metric tons from 176,900; stockpiles dropped to 29,710 tons, with chemical and metal industries receiving the largest allocations.

sections.title: Metal Industries
sections.summary: Pig iron 30,385 tons, rolled steel down to 47,433 tons from the Kyushu power shortage, aluminum 1,016 tons, lead up with Kanioka mine reopened, ferroalloys 1,121 tons.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: 8,409 new coal-miners' houses built since 1 January; October building permits 48,706 for new construction and 53,927 units started.

sections.title: Shipbuilding
sections.summary: Repairs on 473 vessels of 989,325 gross tons from 10 October to 10 November; four steel cargo ships and 14 steel fishing vessels launched.

sections.title: Chemical Industries
sections.summary: Basic chemicals index at 44 percent of minimum requirements; calcium superphosphate 74,583 tons, ammonium sulfate 61,771 tons; critical salt shortage with imports down to 25,178 tons.

sections.title: Machinery
sections.summary: Machine tools 435 units from 53 plants; small tools used 263 tons of steel; industrial machinery output valued at 560,032,000 yen.

sections.title: Railway Rolling Stock
sections.summary: Locomotive output fell; 73 new passenger cars and 95 freight cars built; passenger car repairs up 52 to 1,063.

sections.title: Textile Machinery
sections.summary: September textile machinery output weighed 5,203 metric tons and was valued at 387,562,000 yen, with a shift from repairs to parts.

sections.title: Section 4. Manufacturing
sections.summary: Flour output 157,107 tons, figured window glass made for the first time since the war, small trucks 192 versus 90, toys 7,103,210 pieces, matches at 94.4 percent of schedule.

sections.title: Food Processing
sections.summary: Flour production 157,107 metric tons from 131,648 tons of imported wheat; soy sauce 37,583 tons; brewing cut by lack of blending alcohol.

sections.title: Glass and Ceramics
sections.summary: Window glass up three percent with figured glass at 2,095,300 square feet; refractory bricks 21,546 tons; 17 tons of optical glass melted but none finished.

sections.title: Medical Equipment
sections.summary: Medical instrument output valued at 27,340,000 yen in October, with tables listing items such as 1,572,517 surgical needles and 750 stethoscopes.

sections.title: Electrical Manufacturing
sections.summary: Electrical equipment edged up despite shortages; tables list 3,595,938 flashlight lamps and 31,676 watt-hour meters for October.

sections.title: Transportation Equipment
sections.summary: Standard trucks fell by 133 from 909, small trucks reached 192, tractors 17, light carts 29,527; bicycles dropped 4,932 from 19,143.

sections.title: Agricultural Equipment
sections.summary: 292 producers with 26,771 employees reported agricultural implement output; sickles rose to 234,326 and plows to 18,476.

sections.title: Handicrafts
sections.summary: Lacquerware, silverware and antimony ware rose; antimony ware reached 46,500 pieces after the September floods; 130 ivory factories made 3,820 pieces.

sections.title: Miscellaneous Manufacturing
sections.summary: Wrist watches 31,980, toys 7,103,210 pieces, matches 18,035 match tons, and phonograph records down 174,011 from the postwar high of 869,356.

sections.title: Section 5. Textile Industries
sections.summary: First postwar Indian cotton (712,000 pounds) arrived 31 October with 30,406,000 pounds of CCC cotton; raw silk up 808 bales; export priority for power lifted rayon and woolen yarn.

sections.title: Cotton
sections.summary: Raw cotton stocks reached 52,820,000 pounds; cotton yarn fell 875,000 pounds from power shortages, while cloth output rose 2,045,000 square yards for export.

sections.title: Silk
sections.summary: Raw silk production 10,049 bales, 808 more than September; 277 mills operating; new-crop cocoon receipts 18,407,000 pounds; spun silk yarn mostly down.

sections.title: Rayon
sections.summary: Rayon filament yarn up 301,000 pounds over September; staple trend broken by export restrictions; cloth output down 1,295,000 square yards for lack of yarn funds.

sections.title: Wool
sections.summary: Wool waste stocks rose 379,000 pounds while other raw wool fell; woolen cloth rose 20,000 square yards; worsted spindles operating fell to 58,286.

sections.title: Hard and Bast Fibers
sections.summary: Flax, hemp and jute supplies continued to decline; rope output fell to 1,908,000 pounds from 2,245,000.

sections.title: Throstle-spun and Reprocessed Materials
sections.summary: Throstle yarn output fell to 431,000 pounds from 458,000; reprocessed yarn was 29,000 pounds; cloth output cut by power and labor shortages.

sections.title: Knit Goods
sections.summary: Cotton knit fabric production rose to 1,042,000 pounds for export; yarn receipts fell except export allocations.

sections.title: Clothing and Household Goods
sections.summary: Clothing output fell for lack of fabric and power; cotton cloth stocks in sewing plants dropped from 7,926,000 to 6,941,000 square yards.

sections.title: Sundry Goods
sections.summary: Sewing thread output rose sharply after new price ceilings; fish netting, rope and cordage fell on power and yarn shortages.

sections.title: Dyeing and Finishing
sections.summary: Cotton cloth processed rose to 24,961,000 square yards on export orders; gray fabric stocks fell 1,232,000 square yards; three new mills added.

sections.title: Section 6. Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Buses and trucks registered reached 101,037; rail freight rose 835,200 tons; electric power generated 2,524,000,000 kWh; daily gas production 1,436,903 cubic meters.

sections.title: Section 7. Communications
sections.summary: Nearly 19,000 telephones installed; Great Northern Telegraph licensed 3 November to reopen Nagasaki; domestic mail rose 21 percent to 212,093,843 pieces; Ministry of Communications ran a September deficit.

sections.title: Section 8. Labor
sections.summary: Unemployment laws enacted 21 November, Central Labor Relations Committee ruling of 14 November, Hitachi's 32,000 strikers returned 13 November, and 25,060 unions with 5,840,251 members.

sections.title: Labor Legislation and Policy
sections.summary: Unemployment Allowance and Insurance Laws, Employment Security Law effective 1 December, Labor Standards Law provisions in force 1 November, and a 4,000,000 yen grant for labor-management councils.

sections.title: Labor and Employer Organizations
sections.summary: People's Economic Council of 66 members formed; rally of about 100,000 workers on 12 November; National Congress of Industrial Unions convention 17-20 November; Anti-Communist League formed 7 November.

sections.title: Labor Relations
sections.summary: Government workers' disputes settled by mediation awards; Hitachi, Japan Electric and Japan Radio strikes ended; coal miners demanded 6,270 yen average pay with a 7 December strike deadline.

sections.title: Labor Education
sections.summary: Eleven resident labor schools; five percent of members attended a lecture April-September; Ministry of Labor received about 4,000 books from the U.S. Department of Labor on 29 November.

sections.title: Wages and Working Conditions
sections.summary: The Committee did not uphold the 1,800-yen standard wage; rayon firms agreed to 2,700 yen monthly on 1 November; agreements averaged 2,500 to 3,500 yen.

sections.title: Employment and Unemployment
sections.summary: Seaman retraining funds suspended; textile employment fell 2,109 to 536,391; coal mine employment reached 438,291 at end of October, above the 1945 wartime peak.

sections.title: Public Works
sections.summary: Third-quarter public works certifications reached 980,597,681 yen; the Economic Stabilization Board inspection section made seven inspections.

sections.title: Administration
sections.summary: A training institute for 100 prefectural and local employment security officials ran in Tokyo from 6 November to 5 December, the first of its type in Japan.

sections.title: Section 9. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: 14 import contracts worth $4,104,685 authorized in October; first postwar beans from China (2,690 tons), cotton fabrics exported to the U.S., tractors and shipyard cranes imported.

sections.title: Section 10. Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: Price controls ended on about 200 minor commodities 27 October; staple prices raised 1 November (polished rice 99.00 to 148.50 yen per 10 kg); 132,826 violations reported in October.

sections.title: Section 11. Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Japan notes in circulation about 178 billion yen; Supplementary Budget No. 7 of 85,602,368,000 yen; national debt 321,424,000,000 yen; 22 control organizations closed in October.

sections.title: Money and Banking
sections.summary: Three foreign insurance groups licensed; Bank of Japan note issue 85.2 percent of liabilities; Securities Democratization Committee formed 4 November; 20 life insurers reorganized.

sections.title: Liquidation
sections.summary: 22 control organizations closed in October; cumulative liquidation proceeds to 30 September were 11,937,577,000 yen.

sections.title: Public Finance
sections.summary: Three tax bills, Supplementary Budget No. 7 passed 29 November, government borrowing of 106,257,000,000 yen authorized, and settlers' housing loan ceiling raised to 25,000 yen.

sections.title: Section 12. Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: 378 property reports tabulated; 337 looted ships reported; SCAP dollar custody account 382,399.16; Industrial Recovery Corporation limited 24 November; seven of 17 arsenals inspected by reparations delegations.

sections.title: Property Control
sections.summary: Neutral and Allied property reports totaled 7,562 owners; 1,450 ammonia cylinders restituted to the United Kingdom; property of 914 arrested persons under custody.

sections.title: Antitrust and Cartels
sections.summary: No objection to 466 restricted-concern applications totaling 327,683,925 yen; 30 control organizations ordered closed; Fair Trade Commission hearing notices of 14 November.

sections.title: Reparations
sections.summary: China, Netherlands, Philippines and U.K. delegations accepted 5,289 of 9,745 machines in seven arsenals; 750 items packaged by 30 November.

sections.title: Section 13. Science and Technology
sections.summary: Renewal Committee for the Organization of Science planned a charter for the Diet by March 1948; research grants of 27,853,520 yen; 838 postwar standards; 9 May 1948 eclipse expedition to Rebun Island.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Typhus immunization, Child Welfare Law, 46,589 repatriates, the university chartering committee, and press comment on the budget and coal bill.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Hokkaido typhus booster for 1,256,312 residents, public health train from 1 November, penicillin output 1,605,450,000 units, Child Welfare Law of 21 November, and 46,589 repatriates.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine
sections.summary: Typhus immunization on Hokkaido, a public health train dedicated 1 November, a sanitation committee, and disease charts showing rates fell except diphtheria.

sections.title: Veterinary Affairs
sections.summary: 662 suspected equine encephalitis cases in 28 prefectures; animal diseases other than brucellosis rose; 21,467 cattle slaughtered in September.

sections.title: Medical and Hospital Administration
sections.summary: 3,389 hospitals with 212,100 beds, 97,991 occupied on 31 October; a genetics director for the Atomic Bomb Casualty Commission study was yet to be chosen.

sections.title: Supply
sections.summary: Medical supplies valued at 732,353,544 yen; penicillin up 1,085,790,000 units to 1,605,450,000; typhus vaccine sufficient; laboratory animal breeding set back by the Saitama flood.

sections.title: Narcotics
sections.summary: 87,508 persons registered; 114 narcotics arrests in September; law effective 27 September gave 95 agents power of arrest.

sections.title: Public Assistance
sections.summary: Welfare payments of 358,731,288 yen to 2,947,295 people in October; grants raised 10 percent 1 November; a 686,800,000 yen fund drive began 25 November.

sections.title: Social Security
sections.summary: Unemployment Allowance and Insurance Laws passed 21 November, covering over 7,000,000 workers in firms of five or more.

sections.title: Repatriation
sections.summary: 46,589 Japanese repatriated 31 October to 27 November, 43,424 from Soviet areas; 1,085 repatriates left Japan for Formosa, China and the Ryukyus.

sections.title: Vital Statistics
sections.summary: September births 235,896, deaths 80,036, marriages 72,080 and divorces 7,325; the death rate fell 14 percent from August.

sections.title: Section 2. Education, Religion and Media of Expression
sections.summary: University Chartering Committee approved 18 November, 135,756,768 textbook copies authorized, Shosoin exhibition with 70,000 visitors, first Book Week, and press comment on the budget and coal bill.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: School conferences, University Chartering Committee, scholarship loans doubled 17 November, vocational conferences, and 114,337,886 textbooks distributed by 15 November.

sections.title: Religion
sections.summary: Christian Rural Service and Training Center organized under a 25-year plan; 14 November meeting at the Prime Minister's residence; 30,000 Japanese hymnals shipped.

sections.title: Arts and Monuments
sections.summary: Toro excavation exhibit opened 20 November at the National Museum; third Shosoin exhibition drew 70,000; Nitten attracted 121,105 visitors.

sections.title: Media of Expression
sections.summary: Public opinion conference 24-25 November, first Book Week from 17 November, press comment on Hirano and the budget, 90 Japanese feature films since January, and SCAP library attendance of 19,851.
